# Daniel Arcé
Product engineer who designs and builds accessible software and AI features, from interaction design and prototyping through implementation.

## About
Hello, I'm Daniel Arcé.

I'm a product engineer. I work on products where the interaction model and the technical model are hard to separate: AI-assisted tools, data-heavy interfaces, accessibility-critical workflows, and prototypes that need to survive contact with real system constraints.

### Interactive media, then front-end systems

I started in interactive media and design technology, then spent much of my career building front-end systems for media companies, consumer products, and SaaS teams. That engineering depth changed how I design: I can test an interaction against the actual data model, browser or platform behavior, accessibility tree, and failure states before a handoff turns those constraints into surprises.

### PhotoShelter

At PhotoShelter I combined product R&D with accessibility work on a digital-asset-management platform. I led the WCAG 2.1 audit and remediation for contracts that had to demonstrate compliance, and a workflow-automation prototype surfaced integration problems early enough to cut the later implementation work by an internal estimate of roughly 30%. The [case](/projects/photoshelter/) carries the figures and where they come from.

### Visual Search Workbench and WorkBay

My recent independent work moves further upstream. [Visual Search Workbench](/projects/visual-search-workbench/) is a local-first macOS product for searching and exploring photo libraries with on-device models. [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/) and its adjacent design R&D treat workflow and interaction structure as durable, versioned state rather than information that has to be reconstructed from a chat transcript or codebase on every pass.

### Heuristics Canon

I maintain [Heuristics Canon](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon), a source-linked set of decision rules I use to review product, interaction, accessibility, AI, and engineering work. The useful part is not the size of the corpus; it is that a design claim can point to a rule, a source, and the artifact that changed because of it. The [research note](/research/heuristics-canon/) describes the instrument.

### Senior product and design-engineering roles

I'm most interested in senior product and design-engineering work where ambiguity is real, the interface has to explain complex system behavior, and a prototype is expected to answer product questions rather than decorate them.

### daniel.arce@gmail.com

Send an email about roles or collaboration.

## Projects

### Visual Search Workbench
*Find photos by describing them or starting with a picture*
Year: 2026
Tags: Product Design, Interaction Design, Human-AI Interaction, SwiftUI, Core ML, Accessibility
Summary: A macOS app for finding and exploring photos in your own folders, with search by words or pictures and clear explanations when part of the library is missing.

Imagine looking for a flower photo in a folder of film scans. You remember the pink petals, but the filename is just a number. You could open each scan, or describe what you remember and start from the closest results.

Visual Search Workbench makes that second path possible. It searches the photo folders you choose using words or a reference picture. From a promising result, you can find similar photos, explore the collection by place or date, and save experimental cutouts for use elsewhere.

I designed and built the native macOS app as independent product research. I wanted a useful result to lead to further exploration, with enough context to judge what the search might have missed.

![A search for flowers returns pink cosmos photos from a film-scan library, with one result selected for inspection.](/images/work/sis-search-layer.png)

*Screenshots show version 0.2.0, when the app was called Semantic Image Search. The current download is 0.2.3; the [screen reference](/research/visual-search-workbench-screen-reference/) documents that version.*

## Find a starting point

Start by choosing a folder. The app reads the photos where they are and builds a search index: a separate catalogue it can use to compare pictures. The originals stay in their folders, and the image processing runs on your Mac.

Once the folder is indexed, you can search for something like “flowers” or “red bicycle.” The app compares the meaning of the phrase with the pictures, so a useful result does not depend on someone having named or tagged the file.

Sometimes a picture is easier than a description. Drop a reference image onto the window, or choose **Find similar** on a photo you already have. The results now follow that picture. A banner names the reference image and gives you a way back to the text results, so you can tell which search you are looking at.

![Find similar uses a pink-flower photo as the reference, names it above the results, and offers a Back to text results button.](/images/work/sis-similarity-search.png)

These results are suggestions ordered by similarity. A high position does not prove that a picture contains what you asked for. The interface avoids turning similarity scores into confidence percentages, and it can show “No close matches” when the ranking gives too little useful distinction between results. The nearest photos remain available to inspect.

## Follow the pictures

A useful result can lead somewhere the original query did not. Perhaps a flower photo reminds you of a trip, or its colours suggest a direction for a design. You can explore those connections through **Similarity**, **Places**, and **Timeline**.

**Similarity** groups visually related photos on a map. You can select a cluster and inspect its pictures in the grid. The map is a way to browse neighbourhoods; the size of a gap between clusters is not a precise measure of how different the pictures are.

![The Similarity view groups a 2,314-photo library into a point cloud, with photos in the selected region shown as thumbnails.](/images/work/sis-layers-umap.png)

**Places** shows photos with recorded coordinates. Select a region to find pictures taken there. **Timeline** groups photos by date, letting you narrow a collection to a year, month, or smaller period. It distinguishes recorded capture dates from file dates and keeps undated photos visible as a separate count.

Your selection carries between these views. Their zoom and pan also survive tab changes, so you can examine the same set from another angle without rebuilding your view.

Selecting a photo opens its details, including the camera, capture time, and location when those are available. Those details give you another way to judge whether a suggested picture is the one you need.

## Know what is missing

A photo map can look convincing while leaving out most of a collection. Some files have no location data. Others live on a drive that is unplugged. If the interface hides that difference, you could mistake “the app cannot see these photos” for “these photos do not exist.”

The Places view makes the difference explicit. In one documented screen, it shows 41 of 1,284 photos: 1,198 have no coordinates and 45 could not be read. Those counts explain both what the map contains and why the rest is absent.

An unavailable volume gets a specific explanation. The app names the disconnected drive and says how many photos it could not open. That warning qualifies the dates and places on screen. VoiceOver announces the same warning, using the same wording.

With no folder chosen, the app explains how to start before showing a result count. A search that returns no matches needs a different explanation from one that searched only a partial library because indexing stopped early. With the model unavailable, the app identifies the missing search component so the person can recover.

Thumbnails follow this rule too. A photo that is still loading has a placeholder. A file that is gone is marked “Picture unavailable.” Waiting and failure need different explanations.

## Take a cutout into another project

Once you find a useful picture, the app can separate subjects into layers with transparent backgrounds. You can inspect a layer and save it for composition elsewhere.

![A cat photo has three proposed cutout layers, labelled cat, plant, and left plant, each marked experimental.](/images/work/sis-cat-layers-detail.png)

These layers are labelled **experimental** because a proposed cutout still needs inspection. A recognisable subject does not guarantee a clean edge or a useful separation from its background.

## What I have checked

The app has been exercised on an 8 GB Apple Silicon Mac. Automated tests cover search behaviour and the states described here; expert and adversarial reviews examined the interface, failure handling, and privacy claims. Network checks found no gallery data leaving the device in the tested flows.

A task-based study with outside users has **not yet run**, and larger libraries remain unmeasured. The next evaluation needs to establish whether people can find useful photos and correctly interpret the missing-data explanations.

The [process article](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/) explains how I designed and reviewed those states. The [screen reference](/research/visual-search-workbench-screen-reference/) preserves the detailed drawings and release-specific behaviour.

## Download

**[Download Visual Search Workbench 0.2.3 for macOS](https://dl.darce.xyz/)** — Apple Silicon, macOS 14 or later.

The download is hosted on GitHub. Choose `VisualSearchWorkbench-0.2.3.dmg`, about 295 MB. The search and cutout models are bundled, so no model download is needed on first launch.

The app is **not notarized by Apple**, so macOS may block the first launch. To open it, use **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway**.

The [release page](https://github.com/darce/visual-search-workbench) includes model licences and a `SHA256SUMS` file for checking download integrity. If you use Terminal, put that file beside the disk image and run `shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS`.

### AltContext: Alt Text for WordPress
*Image descriptions informed by the page and reviewed by an editor*
Year: 2026
Tags: Product Design, Human-AI Interaction, Accessibility, WordPress, Vision-Language Models, Python, React
Summary: A WordPress tool that drafts image descriptions using the picture and its editorial context, checks names against confirmed people, and lets an editor decide what to save.

An editor adds a photograph of the founder to a company website. An image model might describe “a person in a red jacket.” The caption supplies a name, but that name could belong to someone mentioned in the article rather than the person in the picture.

AltContext uses the image and the information WordPress holds around it to draft alt text. It checks proposed names against people the site has confirmed, then puts the description in a queue for an editor to accept, change, or reject.

I designed and built the product to make that review practical across a media library. The work is still in development, before public release. The [AltContext site](https://altcontext.com) offers early-access signup.

## Start with the image in its page

Alt text gives people a text alternative when they cannot see an image. What it needs to convey depends on why the image is there. A photograph used to identify the founder has a different purpose from the same photograph used to show a jacket. The [W3C image guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/) explains this relationship between an image and its context.

WordPress already holds clues to that purpose: an image title, caption, filename, and the post around it. AltContext brings those clues into the description request so an editor does not have to re-enter them for every picture.

Those clues can also be misleading. A caption might describe an event without describing anything visible in the photograph. The model is instructed to use the page information as reference material, check it against the picture, and leave out details that conflict with what it sees. Text inside a caption is treated as editorial data, so it is not supposed to become an instruction to the model.

This gives the editor a more informed starting point. It still leaves a judgment to make: does the proposed description serve this image on this page?

## Review a draft before saving it

The review workflow lets an editor inspect generated drafts before applying them to the library. The editor can accept a description or change the wording before saving. Accepting saves the description to the WordPress image; editing saves the editor's version. In this review workflow, generating a draft and applying it are separate actions.

The editor can also mark an image as decorative. That choice is appropriate when the image adds no information that needs a text alternative, such as a purely ornamental flourish. Decorative images use an empty alt attribute, as [W3C recommends](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/decorative/). AltContext keeps that deliberate choice separate from an image still waiting for a description, and does not send decorative images to the model.

The review interface includes a character count and a suggested length of 125 characters. That suggestion does not block saving, and [WCAG does not set that limit](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#non-text-content). The editor still has to decide how much wording the image's purpose requires.

An optional mode also saves a longer description alongside the alt text. Keeping these separate gives an editor room for detail without making every image alternative lengthy.

## Check who is in the picture

A person's identity needs more support than a plausible sentence. AltContext maintains a roster of people the site has confirmed. In the People screen, an editor can review the groups of faces associated with each name and correct groups that have been combined or separated incorrectly.

That roster limits which names a description may use. The system checks whether a recognised face supports a proposed name before retaining it in the text. A name supplied only by the caption is meant to be removed.

Recognition can still be wrong. The automated check gives the editor evidence to review; it cannot settle whether the person was identified correctly. A name that passes the check still needs scrutiny in the draft.

## Keep existing work available

Image recognition and description generation run on a hosted service. The plugin sends images for processing, so this product has a different privacy boundary from an app that works entirely on the editor's computer.

If the service becomes unavailable, the plugin cannot produce new results. Saved descriptions and locally stored results remain available.

A separate connection to a third-party model provider was built for evaluation. That connection is disabled by default and requires an explicit opt-in before images are sent through it.

## What the model comparisons showed

Model comparisons tested whether descriptions used the names supplied in the context. Some candidates produced fluent wording but omitted names. Later evaluations showed that smaller models could preserve them too, so model size alone was not a useful way to choose.

These comparisons helped assess a specific behaviour. Including an expected name does not establish that a model can reject a false one, describe unfamiliar images reliably, or produce useful alt text across a whole website.

An early comparison also exposed a more subtle problem. One draft repeated a caption's claim about a research residency, adding background that could not be seen in the photograph. That example led to clearer instructions about describing the image and avoiding unsupported background information.

## What still needs evidence

Automated checks cover the plugin and service, including accessibility checks on the admin interface. The screens were also reviewed against a written inventory of their actions and states, using the [process described here](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/). These checks help catch implementation defects, but they cannot establish whether the descriptions are useful to the people reading them.

A useful evaluation needs to examine both kinds of identity error: keeping a name that does not belong in the picture, and inventing one when none was supplied. A score for including expected names cannot answer either question on its own.

The product also needs evidence from use. Can an editor spot a wrong description, correct a mistaken identity, and understand what will be saved? Do the descriptions give people who rely on alt text the information they need? The model comparisons and automated interface checks do not answer those questions.

### PhotoShelter: Product R&D & Accessibility at Enterprise Scale
*Product R&D and accessibility for a large DAM platform*
Year: 2021
Tags: Product R&D, Prototyping, Accessibility, Interaction Design, Web Components, OpenCV.js, Enterprise SaaS
Summary: R&D prototyping that cut downstream implementation effort by an internal estimate of roughly 30%, and WCAG 2.1 audit and remediation on contracts worth a combined $9.2M ARR that were exposed if compliance could not be demonstrated, across a media platform serving 80,000+ users and 1B+ files.

## R&D prototyping

Working with the Chief Architect, I built exploratory prototypes outside the production timeline to answer product questions cheaply and catch integration problems before they reached production.

### Workflow automation interface

This prototype informed the [Smart Galleries](https://support.photoshelterbrands.com/hc/en-us/articles/10657698741655-Smart-Galleries) feature. Building it outside the production path surfaced integration issues earlier and reduced development effort by an internal estimate of roughly 30%.

### Client-side image blur comparison

Built with OpenCV.js to test whether image analysis could run fully in the browser without backend resources. The prototype showed that lightweight computer-vision workflows were viable in static-file environments, even though it did not ship as a standalone feature.

## Accessibility

PhotoShelter's customer base includes universities and professional sports organizations, and several key contracts worth a combined $9.2M ARR were exposed if the product could not demonstrate [ADA](https://www.ada.gov/law-and-regs/ada/) and WCAG compliance. I led the WCAG 2.1 audit and front-end remediation effort for PhotoShelter's core product to close that gap.

The initial audit surfaced two classes of issues: fast fixes such as missing ARIA attributes and unlabeled controls, and deeper structural problems such as mouse-only navigation across core menus.

### Keyboard navigation for every menu

![Keyboard navigation for main menu](/images/photoshelter-keyboard-navigation.gif)*Keyboard navigation for the main menu*

Before this work, every menu in the product was mouse-only. Keyboard access is essential for users with limited mobility and speeds things up for power users who prefer shortcuts.

The hardest part was keyboard support across Shadow DOM-based components. Because PhotoShelter relied on Polymer and Web Components, focus and keyboard events did not move cleanly across shadow boundaries. I built a custom layer to bridge those boundaries so interactive elements remained reachable and usable without switching interaction modes.

![The main menu goes from mouse to keyboard control](/images/photoshelter-empty-trash.gif)*Mouse to keyboard control, no mode switch needed*

## Team adoption

I mentored four developers on accessibility patterns and introduced review checklists so accessibility was built into new work rather than added later as remediation.

### WorkBay: State for Coding Agents
*Durable workflow and interaction state for coding agents*
Year: 2026
Tags: Product Design, AI Workflow Design, Developer Tooling, Coding Agents, MCP, Python
Summary: Coding agents forget the work that matters when a session ends. WorkBay makes task, review, decision, and test state durable and portable across agent tools.

A coding agent is a language model driving developer tools: it edits files and runs tests, and it reasons inside a context window, the model's short-term working memory, which vanishes when the session ends. What vanishes with it is the working state of a project: which task was active, which review findings are still open, why a decision went one way, and what evidence backs it. WorkBay keeps that state in the repository, so the next session, in any of the supported agent tools, picks the work up where the last one left off.

## One journey

Work moves through a fixed sequence: a plan becomes a task, the task gets worked, the work gets reviewed, and findings from the review persist until a gate, a recorded check with authority over the branch, decides whether it merges. Every stage writes to one durable record, so the sequence survives any number of session endings along the way.

A cold session loads its active task and continues it. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, grok, and VS Code Copilot all attach to the same record. Re-entry still carries friction: each tool surfaces the record differently, and context that was never recorded stays lost.

## What the record holds

The record is workflow state: it lives in the project, and a new session reloads recorded decisions directly, with no prose recap. Author and reviewer stay separate, so findings carry their own status and commit provenance while merge authority stays with the parent task. The history is vendor-neutral: one manifest keeps commands consistent across tools, and when a chosen backend is unavailable, dispatch stops and reports the failure.

## A map of the product before the code

WorkBay ships a Design Map tool as the `/ux-map` command. It asks for an inventory first: the jobs a user comes to do, the screens they meet, the zones and states inside each screen, the actions available, and the flows that chain them, each entry carrying a reference into the real code. The inventory lives in one JSON file per surface, checked into the repository like any other source.

From that file a renderer emits wireframes and flow diagrams deterministically: the same inventory produces byte-identical output, so a diff in a render means a change in the design. The wireframe below is drawn from this site's own map.

```text
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| Site chrome  [screen]  *                                   |
| Fully-connected escape hatch on every page: skip link, ma… |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| ZONES                                                      |
|   - Skip to main content (nav) states=[default]            |
|   - Masthead wordmark + subtitle → home (nav) states=[def… |
|   - Decorative 3D cube (other) states=[default]            |
|   - Primary nav: home / work / research / about (nav) sta… |
|   - 2×2 theme swatch (form) states=[default]               |
|   - Detail breadcrumb prev / title / next (nav) states=[d… |
|   - Page canvas + main landmark (content) states=[default] |
|   - Footer: name, résumé, privacy, contact (content) stat… |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| ACTIONS                                                    |
|   [secondary] Go home -> landing                           |
|   [PRIMARY] Open about -> about                            |
|   [PRIMARY] Open work hub -> work-index                    |
|   [PRIMARY] Open research index -> research-index          |
|   [secondary] Open privacy notice -> privacy               |
|   [secondary] Toggle light / dark -> appearance            |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| states: default                                            |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
```

_The site chrome screen from this site's Design Map render: a boxed wireframe listing its zones (skip link, masthead, decorative cube, primary nav, theme swatch, breadcrumb, page canvas, footer), its actions marked primary or secondary, and its states._

The artifacts are there so the screens can be argued about before any of them are built. Reviews cite [the Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/), a versioned rulebook whose stable rule IDs make findings checkable later. One critique of [the semantic image search app](/projects/visual-search-workbench/), run by hand against the canon, caught a cancel button wired to a job that could not exist in the state that showed it, filed as a high-severity finding citing the canon rules it broke and the file and line it came from. The repositories that hold maps then guard them like code: tests assert that every label in a wireframe exists in the real interface, and that each screen keeps a single primary action.

## Under the hood

WorkBay stores state in SQLite at `.task-state/handoff.db` and exposes it over MCP, the Model Context Protocol, a standard interface that lets agent tools call external services. Git hooks protect the main branch during development, and a bounded `/offload` command sends a task to an isolated worktree, a separate working copy of the repository, under a fixed token budget, a cap on how much text the model may consume. Optional embeddings add search by meaning over the recorded rows. The memory design has [its own research entry](/research/agent-memory/), the questions agents bring to the record are collected in [a field note from production use](/research/interrogating-agent-memory/), and whether remembering pays for itself is [an open controlled trial](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/).

Installation details and the current schema are in the [WorkBay repository](https://github.com/darce/workbay).

### Apple: iPhone X Launch & Marketing Tooling
*Marketing Engineering*
Year: 2017
Tags: Front-End, CSS3 Animations, Sass, JavaScript, Node.js, Bash, Gulp, Marketing Engineering
Summary: Built launch-critical landing pages, a CSS-animated email campaign, and internal workflow tooling for Apple’s iPhone X release

## iPhone X launch pages

I worked with Apple’s marketing and design teams to build responsive landing pages for the iPhone X launch in November 2017. The work involved translating high-fidelity static comps into pixel-perfect, responsive front-end code under tight launch deadlines.
## CSS-animated email campaign

I prototyped and developed what was reportedly the marketing department’s first CSS-animated direct email campaign. The animations were designed to increase engagement without relying on JavaScript or image-heavy treatments, keeping the email lightweight and broadly compatible across clients. Internal reporting put the open rate well above the department's norm, though the sample size and the definition of an open were never recorded.
## Campaign tooling

The email production workflow was manual and repetitive, so I built a set of CLI tools in Node.js, Bash, and Gulp to automate build, preview, and deployment steps for direct email campaigns. This reduced turnaround time and made campaign production more repeatable.

### MSNBC: Video Platform Prototyping & Launch
*Design technology and rapid product prototyping*
Year: 2014
Tags: Front-End, AngularJS, Drupal, SCSS, JavaScript, Media Platform
Summary: Prototyped and shipped a live video platform under a six-month deadline for a major broadcast news network

## Context

MSNBC.com had recently been rebuilt on Drupal following the Microsoft/NBC split, with [Lullabot leading the broader platform work](https://www.lullabot.com/articles/msnbc-video-and-drupalcon-case-study). Once the main site was live, the network needed a dedicated video experience. The project had a hard six-month deadline and meaningful partner litigation risk if it failed to launch on time.

## The video platform

I prototyped and developed the video section for msnbc.com/videos in collaboration with an in-house team and external vendors. The product goal was continuous video consumption: viewers could watch live or archived segments while browsing related stories and engagement features without interrupting playback.
![MSNBC interface](/images/msnbc-interface.png)

I iterated through multiple working prototypes, proposing and implementing interface patterns in collaboration with stakeholders. The platform launched on schedule.

## CMS contributions

In parallel, I contributed AngularJS components to MSNBC’s in-house content management system, integrating them with the Drupal backend that powered the broader site.

### barbarabeirne.com: Archive Recovery, Rebuild & 2026 Refresh
*Artist Archive / Portfolio*
Year: 2023, 2026
Tags: Web Components, JavaScript, Sass, Rollup, Accessibility, Archive Recovery
Summary: Recovered a photography archive from a defunct Flash site, rebuilt the portfolio, and later rewrote the live site with Web Components

## The problem

Barbara Beirne's photography archive lived entirely inside a Flash website that had stopped working years ago. The original source files and developer were both unavailable. I was brought in to recover the images and rebuild the site from scratch.

## Recovering the images

The images were embedded in a compiled .SWF binary file. I used [FFDec](https://blog.free-decompiler.com/), an open-source Flash decompiler, to extract usable assets from the binary. It took some work to get clean exports, but the tool pulled the full image set.

![Black and white image of three Cambodian teens standing in front of high school lockers](/images/barbara-beirne-extracted-image.png)*Image extracted from a .SWF file using FFDec*

## The rebuild

Future compatibility was the priority, so I built the site with Web Components and Vanilla JavaScript instead of a framework that could age out. The build pipeline runs on Rollup with Sass for styling. The full-screen image carousel and all navigation are keyboard-accessible.

Barbara's images carry a lot of weight. We decided that a minimal, stark design would frame her work best.

![A group of children climbing on a large pile of debris, one waving the Ulster Banner. Image by Barbara Beirne](/images/barbara-beirne-custom-carousel-belfast-8.jpg)

## Client feedback

> "Daniel is exceptional. He was charged with recreating a photo website built initially in Flash that had long been non-functional.
Daniel came up with suggestions and solutions that were beyond what the original site had and brought it all to life.
The site is responsive and works seamlessly on all platforms and browsers.
Most importantly, Daniel is truly a pleasure to work with. He is a great communicator, delivers on time, is a perfectionist -- in the best sense of the word - and is thoughtful and considerate.
I had no references to go by when we hired Daniel and couldn't be more pleased with his work."
>> *Alison Cornyn*

>> *Artist + Co-Founder and Creative Director Picture Projects*

>> *June 13, 2023*

### bauhausdances.org: Visual Identity & Custom WordPress Theme
*Arts & Film (Independent)*
Year: 2023
Tags: WordPress, Custom Theme, PHP, CSS Animation, JavaScript, Video, Accessibility
Summary: Designed a visual identity rooted in the film’s source material and built a custom WordPress theme with self-hosted video

## The design challenge

Filmmaker Debra McCall wanted a new website for her 1982 film recreating Oskar Schlemmer’s Bauhaus Dances. The challenge was to reflect Bauhaus visual language without falling into generic arts-site conventions.

The visual direction grew out of the film’s Hoop Dance sequence, where white rings create stark geometric forms against a dark stage. I used that imagery as the basis for the site’s visual system and interaction language.

![Reinfentanz performance. A dancer stands on one foot with her left foot stretched back, holding five white rings. Two rings form concentric circles near her head, three form concentric circles below her hips.](/images/bauhaus-dances-hoop-dance.jpg)

A subtle ring-based interaction, derived from the Hoop Dance imagery, adds motion without overpowering the content.

## Implementation

I built a custom WordPress theme on top of [Underscores](https://underscores.me/) so the client could manage content independently. The site also uses self-hosted video with caching optimizations to keep load times low without relying on third-party embeds.

## Research

### Memory Outside the Model
*Durable agent state in SQLite, with embeddings as the index*
Tags: Agents, SQLite, Embeddings, Research
Summary: How WorkBay keeps coding-agent memory in a per-repo SQLite database any agent tool can read. Structured rows are the canonical record; semantic embeddings are an index over them.

## A session forgets everything

A coding agent works inside a context window: the bounded transcript the model can see at once. Close the session and everything it understood about the project is gone. The next session starts as a stranger.

[WorkBay](/projects/workbay/), an orchestration layer that runs coding agents across repositories and gives them a durable shared record, answers with a database instead of a bigger window. Every repository it manages carries a file called `handoff.db`. It is a SQLite database, which is to say a real database that lives in one ordinary file, with no server to run and nothing exotic required to read it. Sessions write into it the things worth keeping: decisions and the reasons behind them, review findings and how they were fixed, blockers, verified test results. Each write lands as a timestamped row attributed to the session and agent that made it, so the record doubles as an inspectable audit trail of what was concluded and when. The next session starts from a small packet, a bounded selection drawn out of that record, instead of starting cold.

## An index card is not the book

The rows alone would already be memory, but memory you can only search by the words it happens to use. A question that comes back months later is rarely worded the way its answer was written down.

So selected fields are also embedded. An embedding model reads a piece of text and produces a vector: a list of numbers, usually several hundred of them, that works as coordinates. Each number scores the text along one learned dimension of meaning, and together they place the text as a point in a space where nearby points say similar things. Distance between points stands in for distance between meanings, so asking why an approach was rejected lands near the rationale that rejected it, even if that rationale never used the word "reject."

The vector works like a card in a library catalog: it finds the book, and authority stays with the book. Each card carries a fingerprint of the text it was made from, so a stale card is detectable, and the whole catalog can be reprinted from the rows at any time.

## Layers of authority

What a session knows arrives in layers. The rows come first: they are the record. When you know the words, exact search answers deterministically, through database queries and plain word search. When you only know the meaning, similarity search over the embeddings proposes candidates. Whatever is found gets cut down to a bounded packet sized to fit at the top of a session, a deliberate spend of scarce context on the task at hand.

Similarity search has a failure mode exact search lacks: it never returns nothing. It answers "here is the closest thing I have," and as the index grows, the closest thing is always something. So meaning search runs behind hard filters: the index is keyed by record type and task, and the fence is built into the schema, where no query can forget to apply it. Left unfenced, recall degrades into suggestion.

## The record leans toward failure

Across the repositories indexed so far, review findings make up about four fifths of the embedded entries: what broke, and what resolution survived review. Most of the rest are decision rationales. These are the things a fresh session cannot see and would otherwise re-derive. Anyone building their own version can take the bias before taking any of the machinery: index failures and rulings ahead of summaries.

## Private by default, portable on purpose

The record is private by default. `handoff.db` stays out of version control, because the record holds reasoning traces, and reasoning traces hold whatever the agent saw, including whatever secrets crossed its screen. Crossing a machine boundary takes a deliberate, bounded export of chosen rows.

Because the record is plain SQLite, reading it takes only the file and its schema. A harness, the tool that runs the agent, is interchangeable at that layer: Claude Code and Codex both read the same rows today. The record belongs to the repository. That is portable state, and it should not be mistaken for free switching: moving between harnesses still costs authentication, installation, capability gaps, and re-orientation. The durable record removes one cost from that list, the loss of accumulated project history.

## Where the evidence stands

Daily use is testimony, and testimony is the weakest tier of evidence worth naming. That is the ceiling for any description of a running mechanism. The counterexample sits close to home: the youngest database in the fleet holds a few dozen decisions and has no embedding index switched on yet. What agents actually ask a record like this is read out of production data in [a companion field note on the questions agents bring to the record](/research/interrogating-agent-memory/). Whether remembering saves more than it costs is a causal question, and it belongs to [a controlled trial in The Economics of Remembering](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/), where the claim has a criterion it must survive.

### Five Questions an Agent Cannot Answer from Context
*What coding agents actually ask a durable project record*
Tags: Agents, Embeddings, Research
Summary: A field note from the production records of WorkBay, a system that gives coding agents a durable project record. The questions agents keep asking that no single session can answer, each grounded in what the record holds.

## The record behind the questions

[WorkBay](/projects/workbay/) gives coding agents a durable project record: the decisions, review verdicts, blockers, and test results of every past session, stored as structured rows that outlive the sessions that wrote them. How the record works has [its own entry](/research/agent-memory/); this note reports what it gets used for.

An agent's working memory is its context window, the bounded transcript it can see at once. Close the session and the window is gone. The questions below recur in real work, and every one of them has its answer outside the window. Everything reported here is read from `handoff.db` files in daily production use. The patterns are measured; the claims about usefulness are testimony from that use, and the two are kept apart on purpose. Because the rows are plain structured data, any agent tool can read what another wrote, so one harness can check another's work without inheriting its transcript.

## The questions

### Where is the core problem?

Review verdicts accumulate per repository, and their distribution is diagnostic. One small project stood out precisely because of this: roughly three of every four of its recorded reviews failed. A session working there sees one failing review and fixes it in place; the record sees a streak, and in this project the streak pointed at the architecture.

### Has this fix been found before?

The object of this search is a solution that worked. The record indexes accepted fixes, and it is searched by meaning rather than exact wording, so a timeout guard written in March is findable in July as "the retry bug," even though the two phrasings share no words. When a new finding lands, that search runs over past resolutions before anyone re-derives the fix.

### Are we relitigating a settled decision?

The object of this search is a judgment rather than a piece of code. Before an agent re-opens an architectural question, the decision record is searched. "Why is this site static instead of server-rendered?" was settled once, with reasons; an agent that asks again receives the ruling and cites it, and in use the debate stays closed. The failure this guards against is specific to agents: with no memory of the argument, nothing stops a model from being talked back into a position the project already rejected. Human teams have their own version of the failure, and [the Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/) is the analogous guard for judgment.

### Is "done" actually done?

A claim of completion checks against rows: verified test results and recorded review verdicts, not the agent's own report. The search by meaning covers the softer half of the question, whether a proposed solution was already discussed, because prior discussion rarely reuses the same words. A different model can re-check the same completion evidence.

### What has already failed?

The object of this search is a dead end. Blockers and abandoned approaches persist past the session that hit them. A recurring failure in agent-assisted development is "let me try a different approach," aimed at an approach that already failed, invisibly, in sessions the current model never saw. The record turns that sentence into a lookup.

## Scope

This note does not show that any of this saves money or tokens. Whether reuse lowers what an agent spends is a causal question, and it is the subject of [a controlled trial in The Economics of Remembering](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/).

### The Economics of Remembering
*The cost is measured; the return still needs a trial*
Tags: Agents, Economics, Research
Summary: A production audit shows that durable agent memory is cheap to inject and rich in reusable fixes. A controlled trial still has to measure whether it reduces token spend without lowering outcome quality.

## The claim

[WorkBay](/projects/workbay/) hands a new coding-agent session a bounded packet drawn from the project's durable record: prior decisions, review findings, resolutions, blockers, and verified tests. How that record works is [described here](/research/agent-memory/); this one is about whether it pays. The claim under test is that starting from the packet lowers the total tokens an agent spends per task while preserving the same outcome quality. Tokens are the metered unit of model work, so tokens per task is the closest thing agent work has to a unit price.

The two halves of that claim are in different states. The packet's price is measured; its effect is not. The distinction matters because a cheap intervention can still hurt: it can distract the agent, or surface stale context that steers the work wrong.

## The record settles the cost side

I audited three production `handoff.db` databases from different codebases. Each stores its workflow events as structured database rows, which is what makes an after-the-fact audit like this possible at all.

### The packet is a rounding error next to the task

A compact memory packet averages about 300 tokens. The tasks it precedes range from a few thousand tokens to hundreds of millions at the top end, where a single task fans out across many worker lanes, and the median task lands near three hundred thousand: roughly a thousand times the packet that opened it. Whatever else turns out to be true, the direct price of remembering is not the obstacle.

The costs that could still matter are indirect: retrieval latency, stale or irrelevant context, private state leaving its boundary, worse decisions made with misplaced confidence. None of them appears as a line item, which is why the experiment scores the quality of the outcome alongside the token count.

### The shelves are stocked

For memory to save anything, the record has to hold answers worth retrieving, and it does. Across the three codebases, about 99% of findings marked resolved carry a written resolution a later session could reuse instead of re-deriving; no codebase fell below 97%. The record also holds findings that recur across tasks and findings reopened after being closed, and session starts repeat the same orientation queries. All of it is work that has been paid for more than once.

What this settles is the write path: the library is stocked and the shelving is consistent. Whether an agent pulls the right volume at the right moment, and whether that changes what it spends, is the part production history cannot certify.

### Portability is already in hand

The same record carries rows written by several different agent tools, and any of them can read the decisions and review evidence the others left behind. For a technologist weighing adoption, this benefit needs no experiment to confirm: the audit trail and portable project state exist today, whatever the trial ends up saying about token savings.

## The record cannot settle the benefit

Production history cannot say whether the packet causes savings. Every interactive session receives a packet, so there is no untreated group to compare against. The sessions that meter token spend reliably are the orchestrated worker lanes, and those never receive packets. One instrument has the treatment; the other has the meter. No session has both.

More mining cannot close that gap. The comparison has to be built on purpose, which is what the experiment is for.

## The experiment

Instrumentation comes first. The interactive harness has to record one audited token total per assigned task. The rule that selects and formats the packet has to be versioned and frozen. Each task's type and expected size has to be recorded before assignment, both arms have to start from the same base commit under the same limits, and a reviewer who cannot see which arm produced the work scores it against a fixed rubric.

Then the run:

1. **A/A calibration.** Pairs of identical cold runs establish how much two attempts at the same task differ on their own. That baseline noise sets how many pairs the trial needs.
2. **Content probe.** A relevant packet runs against an equal-size packet from an unrelated project. If relevance is not even detectable, the trial is not ready.
3. **Matched pairs.** Each task runs twice from the same starting commit, one run with the frozen packet and one cold, assigned at random. Fixed token and time bounds keep either side from running away, and neither run writes back to the shared record until its pair closes.
4. **Readout.** The primary metric is total tokens per task, reported as a confidence interval on the paired difference alongside the blinded quality scores. Failed tasks stay in the denominator.

The success bar is set before the first pair runs: the packet has to cut token spend by at least a fifth, while the blinded quality scores stay within a declared margin of the cold arm's. Fixing the bar in advance is what keeps the eventual result honest, because a threshold chosen after seeing the data can always be argued into place. A fifth is where the saving justifies engineering attention. If the measured interval clears it, the claim stands; if it falls short, the claim closes and the packet keeps its job as an audit trail only. The trial covers one repository's workload, so anything broader would need replication.

The stance going in comes from the [Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/) epistemics rule [EXP-01](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/main/lexicons/epistemics.md#exp-01): `require a controlled evaluation … and a prior that most ideas are flat or negative`. Most interventions of this shape do nothing. The audit above justifies running the experiment; it does not justify predicting its result.

## The decision in the meantime

Anyone deciding today whether a persistent memory system earns its keep has settled facts and one open question. The direct cost is negligible against the work it precedes. The audit trail and portability across agent tools are usable today. The material worth reusing demonstrably exists. What stays open until the trial reports is whether reuse lowers spend at equal quality.

My own position is cheap insurance: the packet stays on while the instrumentation lands, since its measured price is small and its side benefits are already real. The controlled comparison decides whether it is also making the work cheaper.

### Designing Search That Explains What Is Missing
*How a screen inventory and explicit review rules shaped Visual Search Workbench*
Tags: Process, Interaction Design, Human-AI Interaction, Research
Summary: A practical account of designing incomplete-data states: map the screens, review the decisions, and check the built interface against both.

On a fresh launch, an early build of [Visual Search Workbench](/projects/visual-search-workbench/) told the person two things at once: choose a folder, and wait while search prepares. It also offered a Cancel button that could not cancel the preparation.

Each message made sense in isolation. Together, they left the person without a clear next step.

That defect is a useful example of the method behind the app. I used three connected practices: **map the states**, **review the decisions**, and **check the built interface**. This is an account of using them on one product; their value beyond this project still needs testing.

## Map the states

A screen has more to communicate than its successful result. A search screen must also explain an empty library, work in progress, an unreadable file, or a missing drive. Those conditions determine what the person can do next.

Before building the interface, I recorded its screens, regions, states, and connecting journeys in a written **UX map**. For each region, the map described what appears when data is missing, loading, partial, or wrong. This made omissions available for review before they became gaps in the app.

Each screen also had a question to answer. On first launch: how does someone start, and will their photos be copied? During indexing: what does a half-finished collection allow the interface to claim? Those questions gave each review a specific purpose.

The map lived in a version-controlled file. Changes could be compared, and the file could be rendered as simple text drawings for discussion. The drawings helped people inspect the layout while the written map remained the place to update the design.

## Review the decisions

A map records a decision, but it does not establish whether the decision is sound. For that, I used the [Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/): a collection of review rules linked to their published sources. A finding could name a rule and explain why it applied, giving me something concrete to accept, challenge, or revise.

Some useful rules came from engineering books. *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* informed how the app treats its search index as a rebuildable copy of information. *Release It!* informed the handling of dependencies that can fail. *Latency* informed the decision to measure slow operations on the target machine.

Those ideas reached the interface through ordinary product questions. If a drive is unplugged, what is missing from the map? If the search model cannot load, what still works? If indexing is unfinished, what does the result count describe?

### Similarity needs an explanation

The search model turns each picture and query into a numerical representation called an **embedding**. The app compares these representations to find nearby candidates. Their usefulness depends on a few constraints that shaped the product.

First, the representations must be comparable. The app uses one defined model and preparation process for its search index and queries. If that definition changes, the index must be rebuilt. The photo files remain the source from which it can be rebuilt.

Second, the nearest pictures are not necessarily good answers. A ranking can return its closest candidates even when none is relevant. The interface therefore avoids confidence percentages. It also warns “No close matches” for a nearly flat ranking while still showing the nearest photos. That check does not establish a reliable relevance threshold for every query.

Third, faster search can introduce its own costs. An approximate search may miss candidates. Measurements on the target machine supported comparing the query with every indexed picture at the tested library size, so that simpler approach shipped. Larger libraries remain an open measurement question.

## Check the built interface

Once the app ran, I checked it against the map again. The [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/) review workflow produced text drawings anchored to the implementation. One drawing exposed the contradictory first-launch state:

```text
┌─ Search ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [ query…                              ] (or drop an image)            │
│                                                                       │
│   No library yet — open a folder to search.                           │
│ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ Preparing search…                                      [Cancel]   │ │
│ │ ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  (indeterminate)                   │ │
│ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    two competing "nothing here yet" messages, rendered at the same time
    this [Cancel] cancels nothing
```

_Search screen as first built: a query field above the message “No library yet — open a folder to search.”, and directly beneath it a second panel reading “Preparing search…” with an indeterminate progress bar and a Cancel button. Two competing empty-state messages are drawn at the same time, and that Cancel cancels nothing._

The two messages were controlled independently. Both conditions could be true, so both messages appeared. The Cancel button reused an indexing action: pressing it recorded a cancelled indexing job even though no indexing job had started.

A nearby state had a related problem. Search preparation and the Similarity layout could show two almost identical progress bars, each with a Cancel button. Their accessibility names distinguished the jobs, but their visible labels did not.

The fix was to make the status region choose one state at a time. The order gives priority to active work, then errors and instructions, before a request to wait:

```text
   indexing ───────►  live work first
   error ──────────►  then why it stopped
   empty library ──►  then what to do
   preparing ──────►  then just wait
   otherwise ──────►  ready
```

_Precedence order for the rebuilt status region, tested top to bottom: indexing shows live work first, then error explains why it stopped, then empty library says what to do, then preparing asks the reader to wait, and otherwise the region reads ready._

The waiting state now names what is loading and offers no Cancel button, because that operation cannot be cancelled:

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ▟▙▟▙▟▙▟▙▟▙▟▙  (indeterminate)                                  │
│ Preparing search   Loading the search model…       (no Cancel) │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

_The rebuilt waiting state: a single indeterminate bar over the label “Preparing search” and the subtitle “Loading the search model…”, with no Cancel button, because nothing in this state can be cancelled._

A unit test checks the combinations of inputs and confirms that this region chooses one state, with Cancel available only for indexing. The [screen reference](/research/visual-search-workbench-screen-reference/) records the other release-specific states, including disconnected drives and unavailable models.

The lesson for a product builder is practical: review the combinations as well as the individual messages. A well-written loading message can still be confusing when another region tells the person to do something incompatible.

## Keep the evidence behind a decision

The review process also needed a memory. WorkBay recorded decisions, their rationale, review findings, and the commands used to check changes. A later session could revisit that evidence instead of relying on a summary that said the work was finished.

Recorded findings still needed judgment. Some led to changes; others were withdrawn or superseded. Keeping the reason for each resolution helped prevent later reviews from reopening the same issue without new evidence.

The build tools used search too. Codemap indexed source-code structure, while local text embeddings helped retrieve earlier decisions and findings. Both produced candidates to inspect against the original code or record. A search result alone could not prove that a feature was absent or a decision had never been made.

That is the same constraint the photo interface has to communicate. A view built from part of a collection must explain what it covers. In the app, that explanation helps someone interpret a map. In the build process, it helps a reviewer judge the evidence behind a change.

## What remains to test

This process found concrete defects and led to testable fixes. It has not yet shown how well people outside the reviews understand the resulting interface. A task-based study is the next step: can someone find a useful photo, recognise an incomplete result, and recover when part of the library is unavailable?

### Heuristics Canon
*Source-linked decision rules for product and engineering review*
Tags: Design Systems, Accessibility, Research
Summary: A working research corpus that turns recurring product, interaction, accessibility, AI, and engineering decisions into checkable rules with stable IDs and source provenance.

## A review instrument, not a style guide

The Heuristics Canon is a review instrument. It forces a claim to name three things before it ships: the rule being applied, the source that earns that rule its place, and the artifact the claim would change. A source can be a published study or a shipped artifact; a rule with no source does not enter the corpus. Source linkage is provenance for the rule, not evidence that users already validated the product.

## The IDs hold still

Rules never get renumbered, so a critique written against an earlier revision still resolves. That is the difference between advice and a corpus you can cite: a design claim points to a rule, the rule points to a source, and the changed artifact records which rule moved it.

## Rules that changed the work

The test of a rule corpus is whether it reverses decisions that were already made. The agent workflow records described in [Memory Outside the Model](/research/agent-memory/) keep those reversals on file, and they are the strongest evidence the canon has.

A review agent once proposed rewriting roughly forty code sites it had classified as defective by a surface pattern. Checked against the canon's measurement rules, the classification itself was probed first; about a third of the sites turned out to be false positives, and the sweep shrank to the handful that were actually verified. In another case, an agent had written a failure into the plan record as if it were live in the shipped corpus. Re-read against the claims rules, it corrected its own entry, noting the failure existed only on an input it had constructed for the test. Both cases share the shape: an agent proposes, names a rule and source, and narrows or withdraws the proposal before a false claim lands.

The same corpus reviews this site. [Visual Search Workbench](/projects/visual-search-workbench/) names CAL-02 and RLSE-04 as the two rules that split its incomplete-data states apart, and that case carried a visible media-pending note until captured screenshots existed to replace it, so it never implied evidence it did not have. The writing rules vetted the research entries you are reading now; earlier drafts lost several rhetorical habits to them.

The corpus is public: [Heuristics Canon on GitHub](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon).

### Visual Search Workbench: Screen Reference
*Detailed interface states for version 0.2.3*
Tags: Interaction Design, Accessibility
Summary: Eight accessible screen drawings documenting search, exploration, missing data, and recovery in Visual Search Workbench 0.2.3.

This reference accompanies the [product story](/projects/visual-search-workbench/) and the [design process](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/). It records the detailed states for version 0.2.3, rather than serving as a step-by-step introduction.

The drawings were checked against the 0.2.3 source. A test in the product repository checks quoted interface strings against their named Swift files. The screenshots in the product story show 0.2.0, before the rename from Semantic Image Search and the thumbnail changes in 0.2.3.

The paths, filenames, and counts below are examples from the documented states. In particular, the missing-model screen shows recovery from an unreadable custom model folder; the downloadable app bundles its models.

## 1. Cold start

**Screen 1 — Cold start.**

The first launch explains how to begin. It does not report zero results before a library exists.

```text
┌─ Visual Search Workbench ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ┌─ Assets ──────────┐ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ ▾ Assets          │ │ [ Search query                      ] (Search) │ │
│ │   Photos you have │ │ [ Add Folder… ]                                │ │
│ │   matted appear   │ │ Choose a folder to search. Your photos stay    │ │
│ │   here. Open a    │ │ where they are.                                │ │
│ │   folder to get   │ ├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│ │   started.        │ │                                                │ │
│ │ ▸ Jobs            │ │                                                │ │
│ └───────────────────┘ └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

_Screen 1, cold start: window with an empty Assets pane reading 'Photos you have matted appear here. Open a folder to get started.' beside a search pane with an Add Folder button and the line 'Choose a folder to search. Your photos stay where they are.'; no result count is drawn._

## 2. Indexing

**Screen 2 — Indexing.**

Indexing reports completed work against a total. Cancelling leaves a partial index.

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [ Search query                                          ] (Search)       │
│ [ Add Folder… ]                                                          │
│ ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░░░░░░░░░░░░  Embedding 812 of 1284…                   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ▢ ▢ ▢ ▢ ▢ ▢                                                             │
│  ▢ ▢ ▢ ▢ ▢ ▢                                                             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

_Screen 2, indexing: an Add Folder button and a determinate progress bar reading 'Embedding 812 of 1284…' under the search field, above a two-row grid of photo placeholders._

## 3. Semantic results

**Screen 3 — Semantic results.**

Results are ordered by similarity. In 0.2.3, thumbnails load four at a time, with a two-second wait limit and staggered retries. A missing file gets a permanent explanation.

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [ red bicycle                                           ] (Search)       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ Explore                                                                │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ red bicycle                                                              │
│ 64 search results · nearest 64                                           │
│  ●  ●  ▢  ●  ▢  ●    ▢ decoding; asks again on a jittered backoff        │
│  ●  ▢  ●  ●  ●  ▢                                                        │
│  ●  ●  ●  ×  ●  ●    × Picture unavailable                               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

_Screen 3, semantic results: query 'red bicycle' with a header reading '64 search results, nearest 64' above three rows of result thumbnails — some decoded, several still placeholders waiting on a retry, and one marked Picture unavailable._

## 4. A photo selected, details open

**Screen 4 — A photo selected, details open.**

File metadata gives the reader facts to inspect alongside the search ranking. The location map uses bundled coastline data and states the area shown.

```text

│ ┌────────────────┐  IMG_4417.HEIC                                        │
│ │                │  Selected photo · double-click to open                │
│ │   [ preview ]  │  ▾ Photo details                                      │
│ │                │        Size  4032 × 3024                              │

│                          Taken  2021:07:14 18:22:00                      │

│                                 ┌──────────────────────────┐             │
│                                 │ ∿∿∿∿   ·   ·      ∿∿∿∿∿∿ │             │
│                                 │  ∿∿∿─────●───────∿∿∿     │             │
│                                 │    ∿∿∿∿∿∿· ∿∿∿∿∿∿∿       │             │
│                                 └──────────────────────────┘             │
│                                 Northern high latitudes, western         │
│                                 hemisphere                               │
│                                 Area shown: 60.15° N–68.15° N,           │
│                                 25.94° W–17.94° W                        │
```

## 5. Explore: Similarity / Places / Timeline

**Screen 5 — Explore: Similarity / Places / Timeline.**

The counts describe different subsets. A location selection can include photos outside the search results; those photos are labelled and listed without a search rank.


## 6. Partial-library caveat

**Screen 6 — Partial-library caveat.**

The warning names the unavailable drive and qualifies the whole view. Visible and VoiceOver wording come from one string.

```text

│   not all of it.                                                         │

│ │      ▁▂▅█▆▃▁    ▁▃▄▂▁      ▂▇█▅▂▁     ▁▂▃▁                           │ │
│ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

_Screen 6, partial-library caveat: an Explore view warning that 312 photos were never opened and that dates and places describe the rest of the library, above a timeline histogram._

### 3D Without Canvas or WebGL
*Rotation matrices with DOM Elements & CSS transforms; no Canvas or WebGL*
Tags: Linear Algebra, 3D Graphics, TypeScript, DOM Manipulation, CSS Transforms
Summary: A browser experiment that makes rotation matrices and perspective projection, normally abstracted by WebGL, visible using only TypeScript, DOM elements, and CSS transforms

> **What this is:** a small experiment showing how 3D rotation and projection map to browser rendering using only DOM elements, TypeScript, and CSS transforms.
> **What this is not:** a general-purpose 3D engine or a recommended production rendering pipeline.

## Why DOM Instead of Canvas?

In this experiment, the cube is not drawn on a canvas. Each vertex is a `div` element, positioned using CSS transforms.

This is a deliberate constraint: no canvas, no WebGL, no engine; just enough code to make the math visible from matrix multiplication to motion on screen.
## The Problem

A cube has eight vertices. Each vertex is a point in space: $(x, y, z)$.

To rotate the cube, we need new coordinates for every vertex—coordinates that place each point in its rotated position.

Rotation matrices perform that transformation. In this demo, the math is done directly in TypeScript and the result is pushed into CSS transforms.

## One Axis at a Time

Rotation around an axis leaves that axis unchanged. Rotating around $z$ moves points in the $xy$-plane. Rotating around $x$ moves points in the $yz$-plane.

Each axis has its own matrix. In the plane perpendicular to that axis the picture is a 2D rotation: counterclockwise when $y$ points up (the math convention), clockwise when $y$ points down (the screen).

### Around X

The first row is $[1, 0, 0]$. This preserves $x$:

$$R_x(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$

```typescript
const rotationX = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [1, 0, 0],
        [0, Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}
```

### Around Y

The middle row is $[0, 1, 0]$. No rotation around the $y$-axis leaves $y$ unchanged while rotating points in the $xz$-plane:

$$R_y(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$
```typescript
const rotationY = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), 0, Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, 1, 0],
        [-Math.sin(angle), 0, Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}
```

### Around Z

The last row is $[0, 0, 1]$. This preserves $z$:

$$R_z(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

```typescript
const rotationZ = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle), 0],
        [Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle), 0],
        [0, 0, 1]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}
```

## Applying a Rotation

To rotate a vertex, multiply the matrix by its coordinates:

$$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ z' \end{bmatrix} = R \cdot \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}$$

The result $(x', y', z')$ is the rotated position. Do that for every vertex and the whole shape turns. The origin stays put.

In this demo, that math is done in plain TypeScript:
```typescript
const matrixMultiplyVertex = (matrix: number[][], vertex: Vertex): Vertex => {
    const result: number[][] = []
    for (let i = 0; i < matrix.length; i++) {
        let sum = 0
        sum += matrix[i][0] * vertex.x
        sum += matrix[i][1] * vertex.y
        sum += matrix[i][2] * vertex.z
        result[i] = [sum]
    }
    return { x: result[0][0], y: result[1][0], z: result[2][0] }
}
```

## Combining Rotations

The cube above uses all three matrices in sequence: $R_x$, then $R_y$, then $R_z$.

This demo uses **column vectors** and $v' = Mv$ (matrix on the left). Composition is right-to-left: apply $R_x$, then $R_y$, then $R_z$. Rotations are **active** (they move the cube; the axes stay put) and **right-handed**: a positive angle is counterclockwise when you look along the axis toward the origin. Screens flip $y$, so the same $R_z$ looks clockwise on the page. The view step later is not a rotation — it is a projective scale.

Order matters. Rotating first around $z$ then around $x$ is not the same as $x$ then $z$. Matrix multiplication is not commutative. Walk it one turn at a time:

A single rotation about an arbitrary axis $\hat{u}$ is the same idea in one step: the part of $\vec{v}$ along $\hat{u}$ is fixed; the rest spins in the plane of $\theta$.

```typescript
export const transformPoints = (
    vertexArray: Vertex[],
    angleX: number,
    angleY: number,
    angleZ: number,
    scale: number,
    eyeDistance: number,
) => {
    let rotatedPoints = rotationX(vertexArray, angleX)
    rotatedPoints = rotationY(rotatedPoints, angleY)
    rotatedPoints = rotationZ(rotatedPoints, angleZ)
    const scaledPoints = scaleXYZ(rotatedPoints, scale)
    return projectPoints(scaledPoints, eyeDistance)
}
```

The goal isn’t to build a general transform stack; it’s to keep the full pipeline visible: matrix multiplication in TypeScript, projection, and DOM updates in the browser.

## From 3D to Screen

After rotation the cube is still in 3D. The screen is 2D.

A ray from the eye through the screen hits the point. Where it crosses the screen is what you draw.

The gap from the eye to the screen is **eye distance** $d$ (the camera's $z$ when the plane sits at $z = 0$). The two triangles — eye to the screen hit, and eye to the point — are the same shape, so **height on screen** is a shrink of **height in space**:

$$\text{height on screen} = \text{height in space} \times \frac{d}{\text{depth}}$$

Depth here is $d - z$. Farther away means a larger depth, so a smaller mark. Same construction as $B_x = A_x \cdot d / A_z$.

The demo stores $d$ as `eyeDistance` and folds the shrink into one **perspective scale** $s = 1/(d - z)$. Same $d$, two depths: the far tree lands closer to the middle, and smaller.

```typescript
const projectPoints = (vertexArray: Vertex[], eyeDistance: number): Vertex[] => {
    const result: Vertex[] = []
    vertexArray.forEach(vertex => {
        const perspectiveScale = 1 / (eyeDistance - vertex.z)
        const projectionMatrix = [
            [perspectiveScale, 0, 0],
            [0, perspectiveScale, 0],
            [0, 0, 1]
        ]
        result.push(matrixMultiplyVertex(projectionMatrix, vertex))
    })
    return result
}
```
This simplified projection works for a small demo, though in a more robust renderer you’d guard against points crossing the projection plane.

Each frame, eight vertices become eight screen positions. Those positions render as the dots you see above.

Again: no canvas, no 3D engine—just math → DOM updates.

### The Render Loop

React manages the vertices as state. When mouse movement triggers a recalculation, the component re-renders with new coordinates:

```typescript
{vertices.map((vertex, index) => (
    
))}
```

The browser handles the actual positioning. We compute the math; CSS does the rendering.

### DOM, GPU, and Seeing the Math

Using `translate3d` lets the browser composite vertices on the GPU. For eight tiny `div`s, that’s plenty: the GPU moves a few layers while the CPU focuses on the math.

This demo isn’t about “beating” WebGL. It’s about keeping the entire 3D pipeline visible, rotation & projection, so you can read the math directly in TypeScript and see the result on screen.

Here's the full chain:

1. Take a 3D point  
2. Apply rotation matrices  
3. Project to 2D  
4. Push the result into a CSS transform

## The complete code

The functions from the article, in one place, in the order the cube runs them. This is `lib/matrixTransformations.ts` plus the vertex `div`s.

```typescript
interface Vertex {
    x: number
    y: number
    z: number
}

const rotationX = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [1, 0, 0],
        [0, Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}

const rotationY = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), 0, Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, 1, 0],
        [-Math.sin(angle), 0, Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}

const rotationZ = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle), 0],
        [Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle), 0],
        [0, 0, 1]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}

const transformPointsWithMatrix = (vertexArray: Vertex[], matrix: number[][]): Vertex[] => {
    return vertexArray.map(vertex => matrixMultiplyVertex(matrix, vertex))
}

const matrixMultiplyVertex = (matrix: number[][], vertex: Vertex): Vertex => {
    const result: number[][] = []
    for (let i = 0; i < matrix.length; i++) {
        let sum = 0
        sum += matrix[i][0] * vertex.x
        sum += matrix[i][1] * vertex.y
        sum += matrix[i][2] * vertex.z
        result[i] = [sum]
    }
    return { x: result[0][0], y: result[1][0], z: result[2][0] }
}

const scaleXYZ = (vertexArray: Vertex[], scale: number): Vertex[] => {
    const scaleMatrix = [
        [scale, 0, 0],
        [0, scale, 0],
        [0, 0, 1]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, scaleMatrix)
}

const projectPoints = (vertexArray: Vertex[], eyeDistance: number): Vertex[] => {
    const result: Vertex[] = []
    vertexArray.forEach(vertex => {
        const perspectiveScale = 1 / (eyeDistance - vertex.z)
        const projectionMatrix = [
            [perspectiveScale, 0, 0],
            [0, perspectiveScale, 0],
            [0, 0, 1]
        ]
        result.push(matrixMultiplyVertex(projectionMatrix, vertex))
    })
    return result
}

export const transformPoints = (
    vertexArray: Vertex[],
    angleX: number,
    angleY: number,
    angleZ: number,
    scale: number,
    eyeDistance: number,
) => {
    let rotatedPoints = rotationX(vertexArray, angleX)
    rotatedPoints = rotationY(rotatedPoints, angleY)
    rotatedPoints = rotationZ(rotatedPoints, angleZ)
    const scaledPoints = scaleXYZ(rotatedPoints, scale)
    return projectPoints(scaledPoints, eyeDistance)
}

{vertices.map((vertex, index) => (
    
))}
```

### Live Order Book: Real-Time Market Visualization
*Streaming top-of-book depth with WebSockets and React*
Tags: React, TypeScript, WebSocket, Binance API, Data Visualization, Market Microstructure, Cryptocurrency
Summary: An interactive guide to bids, asks, spread, and visible market depth using live Binance WebSocket data

## What is an Order Book?

In a marketplace, some market participants want to **buy**, and others want to **sell**. An order book is the _data structure_ that records those intentions: all active buy and sell orders, grouped by price.

Below is a **live view** of Binance order-book depth near the current market price. React and TypeScript handle rendering, while a direct WebSocket connection streams the top 20 bid and ask levels in real time.

---

## How Trades Execute

A trade occurs when a buy order and a sell order cross.

Two basic order types:

1. **Market order**  
   - “Buy now, whatever the best available price is.”  
   - Matches immediately against the best prices on the opposite side.  
   - Consumes liquidity.

2. **Limit order**  
   - “Buy at 93,000 or better (lower).”  
   - Sits in the book until matched or cancelled.  
   - Provides liquidity.

When a market buy arrives, it lifts the lowest ask.  
When a market sell arrives, it hits the highest bid.  
Each match removes volume from those levels and the book updates.

---

*Data streamed from [Binance's public WebSocket API](https://developers.binance.com/docs/binance-spot-api-docs/web-socket-streams). This page is not affiliated with or endorsed by Binance.*
